content: Several pages on Wikipedia utilize Indic scripts to display native representations of names, places, quotes, and literature. These scripts are encoded using Unicode, which supports a variety of Indic scripts. However, to view or edit Indic scripts, your operating system must have Complex Text Layout (CTL) support enabled. Older operating systems that lack complex text rendering capabilities should not be used for editing Indic scripts. Below are detailed instructions for enabling CTL support and inputting Indic text across different platforms and operating systems. Checking for Existing Support To verify if your system supports complex text rendering, compare how your computer displays specific Indic scripts with reference images. If the rendering matches, your system supports viewing Indic text. However, editing Indic text requires additional text entry software. Platform-Independent Support on Mozilla Firefox Indic IME Plugin: This plugin for Firefox (version 1.0 and above) allows users to type in various Indian languages on web pages. It is easy to install and works across all platforms where Firefox or other Mozilla-based browsers are supported. Padma Plugin: For Firefox 2.0 and above, Padma converts several Indic fonts to Unicode, enabling proper rendering of Indian vernacular websites without requiring additional font installations. Windows 95, 98, ME, and NT These operating systems lack built-in support for Indic scripts. Indic text can only be viewed properly in Internet Explorer, provided an appropriate Unicode font is installed. Recommendations: Install Internet Explorer 6.0 for better Indic script support. Mozilla Firefox does not render Indic scripts correctly on these systems unless a modified version is used. Typing Tools: No Unicode keyboard drivers (e.g., Indic IME, BarahaIME) are available for these systems. Users can rely on online typing tools or specialized offline text editors. Windows 2000 Supported Scripts: Devanagari, Tamil. Enabling Complex Text Support: 1. Navigate to Start > Settings > Control Panel > Regional Options > General. 2. Check the box for Indic under Language settings for this system. 3. Insert the Windows 2000 CD to copy necessary files or download a zip file containing the required files. 4. Reboot the system if prompted. Inputting Indic Text: 1. Add the desired language under Input Locale in the Control Panel. 2. Select the appropriate keyboard layout (e.g., InScript or Phonetic keyboards like Baraha). 3. For users unable to download software, online virtual keyboards like dboard can be used. Windows XP and Server 2003 Supported Scripts: Bengali (XP SP2), Devanagari, Gujarati, Gurmukhi, Kannada, Malayalam (XP SP2), Tamil, Telugu. Enabling Complex Text Support: 1. Go to Start > Control Panel > Regional and Language Options. 2. Under the Languages tab, select Install files for complex script and right-to-left languages. 3. Insert the Windows XP CD to install necessary files and reboot if prompted. Inputting Indic Text: 1. Add the desired language and keyboard layout via the Languages tab in Regional and Language Options. 2. Use ALT + SHIFT to switch between keyboard layouts. 3. Additional keyboard drivers like BarahaIME (Phonetic) or IndicIME (Remington) are available for advanced typing needs. Windows Vista Supported Scripts: Bengali, Devanagari, Gujarati, Gurmukhi, Kannada, Malayalam, Oriya, Sinhala, Tamil, Telugu, Tibetan. Viewing Indic Text: No additional steps are required; CTL support is enabled by default. Inputting Indic Text: 1. Add InScript keyboards via the Control Panel. 2. For Phonetic typing, use BarahaIME; for Remington typing, use IndicIME. Mac OS Mac OS 9 and Earlier: Indic script support is available through the Indian Language Kit (purchased separately from Apple). No third-party Unicode solutions are known. Mac OS X: Supported Scripts: Devanagari, Gujarati, Gurmukhi (10.3 and earlier); Tamil (10.4); Tibetan (10.5). Viewing Indic Text: Safari and most Cocoa applications support Indic scripts. Firefox (up to version 2.0) and Carbon-based software like Microsoft Word do not fully support Indic rendering. Inputting Indic Text: 1. Enable specific keyboard layouts in System Preferences > International pane. 2. For Tamil, activate Murasu Anjal or Tamilnet99 keyboards. 3. Use the input menu in the menu bar to switch between layouts. GNOME Supported Scripts: Bengali, Devanagari, Gujarati, Gurmukhi, Kannada, Malayalam, Oriya, Tamil, Telugu, Tibetan. Viewing Indic Text: GNOME 2.8 and later versions support Indic text natively. Inputting Indic Text: 1. Add keyboard layouts via Applications > Preferences > Keyboard. 2. Use the Keyboard Indicator on the menu bar to switch layouts. KDE Supported Scripts: Bengali, Devanagari, Gujarati, Gurmukhi, Kannada, Malayalam, Oriya, Tamil, Telugu. Viewing Indic Text: Inputting Indic Text: 1. Enable keyboard layouts in the Control Center under Regional & Accessibility > Keyboard Layout. 2. Use the KDE Keyboard Tool to switch layouts. Debian-Based GNU/Linux Distributions Supported Scripts: Bengali, Devanagari, Gujarati, Gurmukhi, Kannada, Malayalam, Oriya, Tamil, Telugu, Tibetan, Punjabi. Viewing Indic Text: Indic rendering works out of the box in Debian 4.0 (etch) and later. For Mozilla/Firefox, enable Pango rendering as described under GNOME. Fedora Core 6 and Fedora 7 Supported Scripts: Bengali, Devanagari, Gujarati, Gurmukhi, Kannada, Malayalam, Oriya, Tamil, Telugu, Punjabi. Installing Indic Fonts: 1. Use the package manager to install fonts for specific languages (e.g., Kannada, Hindi). Keyboard Support: 1. Add language support via the Add/Remove Software applet. 2. Fedora provides transliteration and native keyboard support for languages like Kannada. Gentoo Linux Supported Scripts: Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Oriya, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu. Installing Indic Fonts: Compile Firefox with Pango support enabled or use precompiled binaries with Pango enabled. Inputting Indic Text: 1. Configure USE and LINGUAS flags for your desktop environment. 2. Use SCIM or SCIM-Bridge for input method support. Unicode OpenType Fonts If Indic text is not displayed correctly, install Unicode fonts specific to the script: Bengali: SolaimanLipi. Devanagari: Mangal. Tamil: Akshar Unicode. Telugu: Akshar Unicode. Tibetan: Tibetan Machine Uni. Additional fonts are available from the Department of Information Technology, India, and WAZU JAPAN's Gallery of Unicode Fonts.
